pumac-2019-number-theory-b-01.title: Pair up the divisors
pumac-2019-number-theory-b-01.body:
The divisors of $n$ pair up as $d\leftrightarrow\frac nd$, so if $n$ has $\tau$ divisors their product is $n^{\tau/2}$. We need $n^{\tau/2}=8000=20^3=2^6\cdot5^3$.

Try $n=20=2^2\cdot5$: it has $\tau=6$ divisors ($1,2,4,5,10,20$), and $20^{3}=8000$. ✓

**Answer: 20**

pumac-2019-number-theory-b-01.title: Why it is unique
pumac-2019-number-theory-b-01.body:
$n$ divides the product, so $n=2^a5^b$. Its divisor product is $n^{(a+1)(b+1)/2}=2^{a(a+1)(b+1)/2}\,5^{b(a+1)(b+1)/2}$. Matching exponents: $a(a+1)(b+1)=12$ and $b(a+1)(b+1)=6$, so $a=2b$; then $2b(2b+1)(b+1)=12$ gives $b=1$, $a=2$, i.e. $n=20$.

**Answer: 20**

pumac-2019-number-theory-b-02.title: One prime at a time
pumac-2019-number-theory-b-02.body:
Write $a=2^{x}3^{y}$, $b=2^{u}3^{v}$ (no other primes can appear). The lcm condition is $\max(x,u)=5$ and $\max(y,v)=5$.

The number of pairs $(x,u)$ with $0\le x,u\le5$ and $\max=5$ is $6^2-5^2=11$. The same holds for $(y,v)$, so there are $11\cdot11=121$ ordered pairs.

**Answer: 121**

pumac-2019-number-theory-b-02.title: Direct count of exponent pairs
pumac-2019-number-theory-b-02.body:
For the prime $2$: either $x=5$ ($6$ choices of $u$) or $u=5$ ($6$ choices of $x$), and the pair $(5,5)$ is counted twice: $6+6-1=11$. Same for $3$. Total $11^2=121$.

**Answer: 121**

pumac-2019-number-theory-b-03.title: Multiplicativity
pumac-2019-number-theory-b-03.body:
$f$ (the Liouville function) is completely multiplicative, so $F(i)=\sum_{d\mid i}f(d)$ is multiplicative, and for a prime power
$$F(p^x)=1-1+1-\dots+(-1)^x=\begin{cases}1&x\text{ even}\\0&x\text{ odd.}\end{cases}$$
Hence $F(i)=1$ if $i$ is a perfect square and $0$ otherwise. The sum counts the squares in $1,\dots,2019$: $1^2,\dots,44^2=1936$ (since $45^2=2025$). That is $44$.

**Answer: 44**

pumac-2019-number-theory-b-03.title: Swap the order of summation
pumac-2019-number-theory-b-03.body:
$\sum_{i\le N}\sum_{d\mid i}f(d)=\sum_{d\le N}f(d)\left\lfloor\frac Nd\right\rfloor$. Instead, look at a single $i$. If $i$ is not a square, some prime $p$ divides it to an odd power $x$; grouping the divisors as $e\,p^j$ ($e\mid i/p^x$, $0\le j\le x$) gives $\sum_{d\mid i}f(d)=\sum_{e}f(e)\sum_{j=0}^{x}(-1)^j=0$. If $i=m^2$, every divisor $d$ pairs with $i/d$ of the same sign, and the formula above gives $\prod(1-1+\dots+1)=1$. (For $i\le10$ the inner sums are $1,0,0,1,0,0,0,0,1,0$.) So the total is the number of squares up to $2019$, namely $44$ (a computer check of the double sum agrees).

**Answer: 44**

pumac-2019-number-theory-b-04.title: Count the ways via odd divisors
pumac-2019-number-theory-b-04.body:
Sums of consecutive integers (negative integers allowed) of length $L\ge2$ equal to $n$:

- **Odd length $L=2j+1$:** the sum is $L\cdot(\text{middle term})$, so these correspond to odd divisors $L>1$ of $n$.
- **Even length $L=2j$:** the sum is $j\cdot(2c+1)$ where $c,c+1$ are the middle terms, i.e. $n=\frac L2\cdot(\text{odd number})$. These correspond to even $L$ with $\frac{L}{2}\mid n$ and $\frac{2n}{L}$ odd — exactly one such $L$ for each odd divisor of $n$ (the power of $2$ in $L$ is one more than in $n$).

So the number of ways is $2\,d_{\text{odd}}(n)-1$ (removing the length-1 "sum"). We need $d_{\text{odd}}(n)=1010=2\cdot5\cdot101$. The smallest $n$ is odd with exponents $e_i$ satisfying $\prod(e_i+1)=1010$:
- $3^{1009}$; $3^{504}5$, $3^{201}5^4$, $3^{100}5^9$; $3^{100}5^4\cdot7$.

The last is smallest ($3^{100}5^9$ vs $3^{100}5^4\cdot 7$: $5^5>7$; and the others have far larger powers of $3$). So $n=3^{100}\cdot5^4\cdot7$, a product of $100+4+1=105$ primes.

**Answer: 105**

pumac-2019-number-theory-b-04.title: Formula via factor pairs
pumac-2019-number-theory-b-04.body:
$n=a+(a+1)+\dots+(a+L-1)$ gives $2n=L(2a+L-1)$: the two factors $L$ and $M=2a+L-1$ have opposite parity, and every factorisation $2n=L\cdot M$ into factors of opposite parity gives a valid $a=\frac{M-L+1}{2}$ (any integer). If $n=2^e m$ with $m$ odd, the opposite-parity factorisations of $2n$ are: choose the odd divisor $d\mid m$ and put $2^{e+1}$ on one side or the other: $2d_{\text{odd}}(n)$ ordered pairs $(L,M)$ with $L\ge1$. Exclude $L=1$: $2d_{\text{odd}}(n)-1$ ways (a computer check for $n<300$ agrees). As before $d_{\text{odd}}(n)=1010$ and the minimum is $3^{100}5^4 7$, so $k=105$.

**Answer: 105**

pumac-2019-number-theory-b-05.title: The run must straddle a multiple of 100
pumac-2019-number-theory-b-05.body:
Let $s(n)$ be the digit sum.

**After a multiple of 100.** For $100y,\,100y+1,\dots,100y+19$ the digit sums are $s(y)+0,\dots,s(y)+10$ (the last two digits contribute $0,\dots,9$ and then $1,\dots,10$) — 11 consecutive values, one of which is divisible by 11. Similarly for $100x+80,\dots,100x+99$ the last two digits contribute $8,9,\dots,18$, again 11 consecutive values. Also, 30 consecutive numbers inside one century always contain 12 consecutive digit-sum values.

So a good run of 38 must cross a multiple of $100$, use at most $19$ numbers on each side, hence it is exactly $100x+81,\dots,100x+118$.

**Conditions.** Before the boundary the sums are $s(x)+9,\dots,s(x)+18$, so we need $s(x)\equiv 3\pmod{11}$. After it, the sums are $s(x+1)+0,\dots,s(x+1)+9$, so $s(x+1)\equiv1\pmod{11}$. If $x$ ends in exactly $k$ nines, $s(x+1)=s(x)-9k+1$, so $3-9k+1\equiv1$, i.e. $9k\equiv3$, $k\equiv4\pmod{11}$. The smallest $x$ ending in four nines with $s(x)\equiv 3$ is $x=9999$ ($s=36\equiv3$). The run starts at $999981$.

**Answer: 999981**

pumac-2019-number-theory-b-05.title: Check the run
pumac-2019-number-theory-b-05.body:
From $999981$ to $999989$ the digit sums are $45,\dots,53$, and from $999990$ to $999999$ they are $45,\dots,54$. All lie in $45..54$, which contains no multiple of $11$ ($44$ and $55$ are outside). From $1000000$ to $1000018$ the digit sums are $1,\dots,10$, again no multiple of 11. The neighbours $999980$ ($s=44$) and $1000019$ ($s=11$) are bad, so this run has exactly 38 numbers, and a computer search confirms no earlier run of 38 exists.

**Answer: 999981**

pumac-2019-number-theory-b-06.title: Official approach: odd power sums
pumac-2019-number-theory-b-06.body:
Let $p=101$. Condition (a) with $n=0$ gives $f(0)=1$, and in general $f(x)-1$ is an odd polynomial, so $f(x)=1+ax+g(x)$ where $g$ contains only odd powers $x^3,x^5,\dots$.

The official solution uses the fact: for $m=2k+1\ge3$, $p^2\mid 1^m+2^m+\dots+(p-1)^m$, from $j^m+(p-j)^m\equiv m\,j^{m-1}p\pmod{p^2}$ and summing over $j$. Granting this, $p^2\mid g(0)+\dots+g(100)$, so
$$f(0)+\dots+f(100)\equiv p+a\cdot\frac{p(p-1)}{2}\pmod{p^2}.$$
So $p+50pa\equiv0\pmod{p^2}$, i.e. $1+50a\equiv0\pmod{101}$, $a\equiv2\pmod{101}$. Then $f(101)=1+101a+g(101)\equiv1+101a\equiv1+202=203\pmod{101^2}$ (every term of $g(101)$ is divisible by $101^3$).

**Answer: 203**

pumac-2019-number-theory-b-06.title: A caveat about the key fact
pumac-2019-number-theory-b-06.body:
The power-sum fact above needs $\sum_{j=1}^{p-1}j^{m-1}\equiv0\pmod p$, which holds unless $(p-1)\mid(m-1)$. For $m=201,301,\dots$ (with $101\nmid m$) it fails: e.g. $\sum_{j=1}^{100}j^{201}\equiv5151\pmod{101^2}$. So if $f$ is allowed such terms, $a$ is not forced: for instance $f(x)=1+99x^{201}+x^{2019}$ satisfies both conditions but $f(101)\equiv1$. The intended answer (assuming the coefficients in those exceptional degrees do not interfere, e.g. $f(x)=1+ax+cx^{2019}$) is $203$; e.g. $f(x)=1+2x+x^{2019}$ satisfies both conditions and $f(101)\equiv203\pmod{101^2}$.

**Answer: 203** (official)

pumac-2019-number-theory-b-07.title: Closed form
pumac-2019-number-theory-b-07.body:
Exactly $2^k$ values of $i$ have $\lfloor\log_2 i\rfloor=k$ (namely $2^k\le i<2^{k+1}$), so
$$f(2^{r+1}-1)=\sum_{k=0}^{r}k\,2^k=(r-1)2^{r+1}+2 .$$
Write $n=2^{r+1}-1+m$ with $0\le m<2^{r+1}$; the extra $m$ terms are each $r+1$, so $f(n)=(r-1)2^{r+1}+2+m(r+1)$. Subtracting $(r-1)n$:
$$n\mid f(n)\iff n\mid f(n)-(r-1)n=2m+r+1 .$$
Since $0<2m+r+1<2n$, this forces $2m+r+1=n=2^{r+1}-1+m$, i.e. $m=2^{r+1}-r-2$ and
$$n=2^{r+2}-r-3 .$$
These are $1, 5, 12, 27, \dots$, and the largest below $2018$ is $r=8$: $2^{10}-11=1013$ (next: $2^{11}-12=2036$).

**Answer: 1013**

pumac-2019-number-theory-b-07.title: Verify $n=1013$ directly
pumac-2019-number-theory-b-07.body:
For $n=1013$: $f(511)=\sum_{k=0}^{8}k2^k=7\cdot512+2=3586$, and the numbers $512,\dots,1013$ ($502$ of them) each contribute $9$: $f(1013)=3586+4518=8104=8\cdot1013$. ✓ A computer scan of all $n<2018$ confirms $1013$ is the largest.

**Answer: 1013**

pumac-2019-number-theory-b-08.title: Compact means $a^n\equiv1$ for every unit
pumac-2019-number-theory-b-08.body:
**Necessary.** For any $a$ coprime to $2019$, Dirichlet's theorem gives infinitely many primes $\equiv a\pmod{2019}$; using only those, any $n$ of them multiply to $a^n$. So compact $\Rightarrow a^n\equiv1$ for all units $a$.

**Sufficient.** Given any sequence of distinct primes, drop the finitely many dividing $2019$; some residue $a$ occurs infinitely often, and $n$ primes with that residue give $a^n\equiv1$.

So $n$ is compact iff $n$ is a multiple of the exponent of the group $(\mathbb Z/2019)^\times$. As $2019=3\cdot673$, this exponent is $\operatorname{lcm}(2,672)=672$ (take $a$ a primitive root mod both $3$ and $673$ by CRT to see $672$ is needed).

The compact numbers below $4038$ are $672k$ for $k=1,\dots,6$ ($6\cdot672=4032$), with sum $672\cdot21=14112$.

**Answer: 14112**

pumac-2019-number-theory-b-08.title: Check the exponent
pumac-2019-number-theory-b-08.body:
By Fermat, $a^{2}\equiv1\pmod3$ and $a^{672}\equiv1\pmod{673}$ for $a$ coprime to $2019$, so $a^{672}\equiv1\pmod{2019}$. Conversely, a primitive root $g$ mod $673$ has order $672$, so no smaller $n$ (and only multiples of $672$) can work. A computer search for the least $n$ with $a^n\equiv1\pmod{2019}$ for all units also gives $672$. Sum: $672(1+2+\dots+6)=14112$.

**Answer: 14112**
